content.text: {"primary_meaning": "In mainstream Christian teaching, 'life' (especially 'the life,' Greek zōē) symbolizes eternal, divine life given by God through Jesus Christ — a qualitatively different existence from mere biological life, consisting in saving relationship and union with God, beginning now and consummated in resurrection. In Johannine usage 'the Life' is also a christological title: Christ himself is the embodiment and source of this life.", "primary_basis": ["John 14:6 ('I am the way, and the truth, and the life')", "John 11:25 ('I am the resurrection and the life')", "John 1:4 ('In him was life, and the life was the light of men')", "John 10:10 ('I came that they may have life, and have it abundantly')", "John 3:16 ('whoever believes in him should not perish but have eternal life')", "John 17:3 ('this is eternal life, that they know you, the only true God')", "1 John 5:11-12 ('God gave us eternal life, and this life is in his Son; whoever has the Son has life')", "Colossians 3:4 ('Christ who is your life')", "John 5:24-26; 6:35, 48 (bread of life)", "Romans 6:4, 23 ('newness of life'; 'the gift of God is eternal life')"], "alternatives": [{"meaning": "Christological title: 'the Life' refers to the person of Christ himself as the source and embodiment of divine life, not merely a gift he confers.", "basis": ["John 14:6", "John 11:25", "John 1:4", "1 John 1:1-2 ('the word of life... the life was made manifest')", "Colossians 3:4"], "prominence": "dominant"}, {"meaning": "Futurist eschatological reading: 'life' primarily denotes resurrection existence in the age to come (immortality, life after death), with less emphasis on present possession.", "basis": ["Daniel 12:2", "Matthew 25:46", "Mark 10:30 ('in the age to come eternal life')", "1 Corinthians 15:22, 42-54", "Revelation 21:4; 22:1-2"], "prominence": "common"}, {"meaning": "Realized-eschatology reading: eternal life is a present spiritual quality — knowing God now, new birth, abundant living — emphasized in Johannine scholarship and in pietist/evangelical devotional teaching.", "basis": ["John 17:3", "John 5:24 ('has passed from death to life')", "John 10:10", "John 3:3-6 (new birth)", "Galatians 2:20"], "prominence": "common"}, {"meaning": "Tree of Life / Edenic symbolism: 'life' as access to immortality and communion with God lost in Eden and restored in Christ and the New Jerusalem; wisdom traditions also call Torah/wisdom a 'tree of life.'", "basis": ["Genesis 2:9; 3:22-24", "Proverbs 3:18; 11:30", "Revelation 2:7; 22:2, 14, 19"], "prominence": "common"}, {"meaning": "Covenantal choice reading: 'life' as covenant blessing and obedience set against death/curse — choosing God's way (Deuteronomic and wisdom framing).", "basis": ["Deuteronomy 30:15-20 ('choose life')", "Proverbs 4:4, 22-23", "Leviticus 18:5", "Psalm 16:11"], "prominence": "common"}, {"meaning": "Participation/theosis reading (Eastern Orthodox and some Catholic theology): 'life' as sharing in the divine nature and energies of God, mediated sacramentally (especially the Eucharist).", "basis": ["2 Peter 1:4", "John 6:53-57 ('unless you eat the flesh of the Son of Man... you have no life in you')", "John 1:4", "Genesis 2:7"], "prominence": "minority"}, {"meaning": "Anthropological/physical reading: 'life' as breath, soul, or blood — the animating principle of creatures (nephesh, ruach), sometimes treated symbolically in atonement contexts ('the life is in the blood').", "basis": ["Genesis 2:7", "Leviticus 17:11, 14", "Job 33:4", "Ecclesiastes 12:7"], "prominence": "minority"}], "has_settled_consensus": true, "confidence": "high", "notes": "There is broad, recognizable consensus across Catholic, Orthodox, and Protestant traditions that 'life'/'the life' in its symbolic-theological sense means eternal divine life (zōē) received through Christ, with the definite-article form ('the Life') widely read as a title of Christ himself, chiefly from John 14:6 and 11:25. The main interpretive variation concerns emphasis rather than substance: present possession vs. future resurrection, personal relationship vs. sacramental participation, and gift vs. person. Scholarly discussion also distinguishes Greek zōē (divine/eternal life), bios (earthly livelihood), and psychē (soul-life), a distinction popularized in commentaries though sometimes overstated in devotional literature. None of these alternatives displaces the core consensus."}
